newsitem.title: FRANCE: JOBS-Record unemployment gnaws at French spirit.
newsitem.headline: JOBS-Record unemployment gnaws at French spirit.

text.p: Thirty years ago, the promise of work in thriving textile mills unable to meet burgeoning demand drew Medhi Kadri's parents and thousands of others from north Africa to northeastern France.
But a generation later, Kadri, 23, is out of work and has little hope that he or his friends will soon find productive jobs.
"People are more or less discouraged," Kadri said, while sipping a glass of juice one recent evening at Chez Lassad, a sandwich shop in the former industrial town of Roubaix.
Most of the mills that kept his parents working have closed, the once busy workforce idled as mines were exhausted and textile production moved abroad to other, cheaper markets.

The experience of the Kadri family and thousands like them, both immigrants and natives, is emblematic of the troubles faced by an entire nation trying to come to grips with the effects of change in the world economy.

Observers say France's unemployment scourge has many origins, both economic and cultural. Its rise in recent years to nearly 13 percent of the economically active population has sparked protest and soul searching by workers, employers and politicians.
But despite political promises, government-funded industry bailouts and a host of special initiatives, a solution remains elusive.
MORE PAIN BEFORE RATE REVERSES
Private economists predict unemployment, already a record 12.7 percent, will rise this year to 13 percent before receding to around 12 percent. It is expected to stay there through 1998.

Critics say relatively high payroll charges, a tax structure that favours business investment in machines rather than people, competition from foreign companies not bound by France's strict labour laws and poor political leadership have all contributed to the problem.
But so has a resistance to change born partly of a feeling in France that an economic system should be more than just a means for people and companies to maximise profits.

The situation has been complicated by Europe's race toward monetary union, which with its tough economic criteria places severe financial restraints on France's traditionally interventionist government.
Emmanuel Todd, noted demographer and self-described "fanatic" opponent of a single currency, attributed a big part of the problem to France being caught between different systems.

It was, he said, caught between the economic system of Germany, with its obsession over anti-inflation policy and a strong currency, and that of Britain and the United States, with an emphasis on economic growth and job creation at the expense of security.
"There is coherence to the U.S. attitude and there is coherence to the German attitude, but the French have taken some of each model and this has caused a problem," Todd said in a recent interview.
As examples he cited France's acceptance of German-style monetary policy, aimed at maintaining a strong franc, while at the same time adopting greater freedom for its financial markets.
"Unemployment and economic crisis in France are two parts due to difficulties France is encountering in its adjustment to globalisation and one part due to the construction of Europe," Todd said.

He blames the adjustment problems on failure by the French political and administrative elite to reform coherently the economy in a manner consistent with its cultural dynamic, not on an inborn reluctance to change.
"France is in crisis not because it cannot reform, but rather because it has not managed to define a programme of reforms that matches its culture," he said.
SINGLE CURRENCY DEMANDS, FRENCH CULTURE SAID UNSUITED

Todd believes the quest for a single currency should be abandoned because it is forcing France into an economic mould for which its culture is not suited. He is also critical because, he says, it strips France of its monetary autonomy.

The view that France needs to craft an economic model matched with its culture is reminiscent of one expressed last year by French President Jacques Chirac, who called for a "third way" between the European mixed economy and the free-wheeling, flexible capitalism espoused by Britain and the United States.
But Todd, who said Chirac's poor political leadership is partly to blame for problems plaguing France, scorns such talk.
"There is no middle way, there are as many ways as there are national cultures."
Up in Roubaix, job uncertainty has extended beyond the ranks of young and unemployed to those with once secure, long-term positions.
Unemployment in this previously prosperous centre has reached 35 percent in some neighborhoods and pessimism over the future has taken hold.

Michel Lagaisse, a native of the region, remembers better times, when there was full employment and Roubaix's position near the Belgian border made it better known as an industrial centre than as the drug transit point it has become.

Stroking his salt and pepper beard and nursing a beer in Le Piree, a well-appointed cafe just across the street from Chez Lassad, Lagaisse -- though his background could not be more different than Kadri's -- expresses the same lack of hope as the second generation of immigrants.
"As long as they continue to replace people with machines, it's going to get worse."
